source_evidence.observation: The problem has n+1 distinct interpolation points x_j indexed by j=0:n, data f_j, an interpolating polynomial p_n of degree at most n, fixed nodes and evaluation point x, and a varying data vector f.
For p_n(x) nonzero, cond(x,n,f) is defined using componentwise relative perturbations |Delta f| <= epsilon|f| and equals sum_{j=0}^n |ell_j(x)f_j|/|p_n(x)|, which is at least 1.
The direct barycentric weights are w_j = 1/product_{k != j}(x_j-x_k).

Each basic operation satisfies fl(a op b)=(a op b)(1+delta)^(+/-1), |delta|<=u, for op in {+,-,*,/}; u is unit roundoff. The relative-error counter is angle(k)=product_{i=1}^k(1+delta_i)^{rho_i}, with rho_i in {+1,-1}, and |angle(k)-1|<=gamma_k=ku/(1-ku), assuming ku<1.
The nodes x_i, data f_i, and evaluation point x are assumed to be floating-point numbers, and directly computed weights satisfy w_hat_j=w_j angle(2n)_j for j=0:n.

source_evidence.anchor: proof of Lemma 3.1 and proof of Theorem 3.2
source_evidence.observation: A direct weight uses n subtraction errors, n-1 multiplication errors, and one division error. The evaluation analysis assigns three local errors to subtraction, division, and multiplication and n errors to summation, with the summation count asserted for any ordering.
The selected algorithm is the second or proper barycentric formula: p_n(x)=[sum_{j=0}^n w_j f_j/(x-x_j)]/[sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)].

source_evidence.anchor: display beginning 'Working in the same way as in the proof of Theorem 3.2'
source_evidence.observation: The computed quotient is represented first with weight counters angle(2n)_j, numerator counters angle(n+3)_j, denominator counters angle(n+2)_j, and one outer-division counter, and then as a numerator with angle(3n+4)_j divided by a denominator with angle(3n+2)_j.

source_evidence.anchor: rewriting of equation (2.2) immediately before Theorem 4.1
source_evidence.observation: The data condition number is rewritten as [sum_{j=0}^n |w_j f_j/(x-x_j)|]/|sum_{j=0}^n w_j f_j/(x-x_j)|.

The relative forward error is bounded by (3n+4)u times the data-conditioned numerator ratio plus (3n+2)u times the denominator-cancellation ratio, plus O(u^2). These ratios are respectively cond(x,n,f) and cond(x,n,1), where 1 is the constant-one function.
The paper additionally asserts existence of rounding errors for which the bound is attained within a constant factor.

binders: The indexing j=0:n and the phrase 'degree at most n' implicitly make n a nonnegative integer and give n+1 data-node pairs; n is not separately quantified in the displayed theorem. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph and eq. (2.1)]

The nodes x_0,...,x_n are distinct and fixed, the evaluation point x is fixed, and the data vector f=(f_0,...,f_n) is the varying input for conditioning. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph]

The theorem concerns the exact interpolant value p_n(x) and the computed value p_hat_n(x) produced from the second barycentric formula. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1); PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]

The rounding model binds one delta per modeled arithmetic operation with |delta|<=u; no independence or probabilistic interpretation is imposed. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model and eq. (3.3)]
hypotheses: The interpolation points x_j are pairwise distinct. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph]
The nodes x_i, data values f_i, and evaluation point x are floating-point numbers. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), paragraph immediately before Lemma 3.1]
The arithmetic obeys fl(a op b)=(a op b)(1+delta)^(+/-1), |delta|<=u, for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model]

The generic counter bound assumes ku<1 for the relevant counter length k, although Theorem 4.1 does not restate a specific inequality such as (3n+4)u<1. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), definition of gamma_k and sentence 'where ku < 1 is assumed'; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]

Because both Definition 2.1 and Theorem 4.1 divide by p_n(x), the normalized claim inherits the requirement p_n(x) != 0. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
The weights used by the analyzed computation are obtained directly from w_j=1/product_{k != j}(x_j-x_k), leading to w_hat_j=w_j angle(2n)_j. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2) and Lemma 3.1]
conclusions: Before collecting counters, the computed value has the form p_hat_n(x)=([sum_{j=0}^n (w_j angle(2n)_j/(x-x_j)) f_j angle(n+3)_j]/[sum_{j=0}^n (w_j angle(2n)_j/(x-x_j)) angle(n+2)_j]) angle(1). [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), display beginning 'Working in the same way as in the proof of Theorem 3.2']

After collecting counters, p_hat_n(x)=[sum_{j=0}^n (w_j/(x-x_j)) f_j angle(3n+4)_j]/[sum_{j=0}^n (w_j/(x-x_j)) angle(3n+2)_j]. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), second equality in the computed-expression display]

|p_n(x)-p_hat_n(x)|/|p_n(x)| <= (3n+4)u A_f +(3n+2)u A_1+O(u^2), where A_f=[sum_{j=0}^n |(w_j/(x-x_j))f_j|]/|sum_{j=0}^n (w_j/(x-x_j))f_j| and A_1=[sum_{j=0}^n |w_j/(x-x_j)|]/|sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)|. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1 through eq. (4.2)]

Equivalently, |p_n(x)-p_hat_n(x)|/|p_n(x)| <= (3n+4)u cond(x,n,f)+(3n+2)u cond(x,n,1)+O(u^2), with the argument 1 denoting the constant-one function. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eq. (4.3) and following sentence]
The paper asserts that there exist rounding errors for which this bound is attained within a constant factor. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
definitions_and_conventions: The exact interpolant is p_n(x)=sum_{j=0}^n f_j ell_j(x), where ell_j(x)=product_{k=0,k!=j}^n(x-x_k)/product_{k=0,k!=j}^n(x_j-x_k). [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), eq. (2.1)]

The direct barycentric weight is w_j=1/product_{k!=j}(x_j-x_k), with the product inherited over the other indices among 0,...,n. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2); PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), indexing in eq. (2.1)]
The second or proper barycentric formula is p_n(x)=[sum_{j=0}^n w_j f_j/(x-x_j)]/[sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)]. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1)]

For p_n(x) != 0, cond(x,n,f) is the limiting worst relative change in p_f(x) under componentwise perturbations |Delta f|<=epsilon|f|, and Lemma 2.2 evaluates it as sum_{j=0}^n |ell_j(x)f_j|/|p_n(x)|. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1 and Lemma 2.2, eq. (2.2)]

The notation angle(k)_j denotes a product of k factors (1+delta_i)^{rho_i}, rho_i in {+1,-1}, whose constituent rounding errors may depend on j. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.3) and following paragraph]
The argument 1 in cond(x,n,1) means the interpolation data are the constant value 1, not a scalar norm index. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
implicit_context: The condition-number framework fixes the nodes and evaluation point and measures sensitivity only with respect to the data vector f. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph and Definition 2.1]

The exact symbols w_j and p_n(x) denote mathematical weights and the exact interpolant, while w_hat_j and p_hat_n(x) denote floating-point computed quantities. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), Lemma 3.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]

Theorem 4.1 inherits operation counts from the direct-weight analysis and from the proof of Theorem 3.2 through the explicit statement that the barycentric calculation is analyzed in the same way. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 550), proof of Theorem 3.2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), paragraph preceding the computed-expression display]

No assumption x_j in [-1,1] belongs to Theorem 4.1; that restriction is introduced only afterward for the Lebesgue-constant corollary. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), paragraph beginning 'To gain more insight']
statement.algorithm_linkage: The result is specifically for floating-point evaluation of the second or proper barycentric formula (4.1), using weights directly computed from (3.2). [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2) and Lemma 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1)] The inherited counting gives angle(2n)_j for each weight, angle(n+3)_j for each numerator path, angle(n+2)_j for each denominator path, and angle(1) for the final quotient; collecting these gives numerator and denominator counters angle(3n+4)_j and angle(3n+2)_j. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 550), operation-count discussion; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), exact computed-expression display]
numerical_model: For op in {+,-,*,/}, fl(a op b)=(a op b)(1+delta)^(+/-1) with |delta|<=u, where u is unit roundoff. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model]
A length-k relative-error counter satisfies |angle(k)-1|<=gamma_k=ku/(1-ku), under the stated assumption ku<1. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.3) and following sentence]
The inputs x_i, f_i, and x are assumed already to be floating-point numbers. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), final sentence before Lemma 3.1]
The theorem uses a first-order expansion in u with explicit linear coefficients and an unexpanded O(u^2) remainder. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
error_notions: The principal error is scalar relative forward error, |p_n(x)-p_hat_n(x)|/|p_n(x)|. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
cond(x,n,f) measures componentwise relative sensitivity to perturbations of f, not perturbations of x or the nodes. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1 and Section 2 opening paragraph]
The second condition term measures cancellation in the denominator sum and equals cond(x,n,1). [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3) and following explanatory paragraph]

The exact counter representation is stated not to admit a useful backward-error interpretation; the theorem instead derives a forward-error bound. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), paragraph following the computed-expression display]
norms: All displayed theorem errors and cancellation ratios use scalar absolute value. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1 and eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
The perturbation inequality |Delta f|<=epsilon|f| is interpreted componentwise. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph and Definition 2.1]
No vector norm is used in Theorem 4.1 itself. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1 through eq. (4.3)]
constants_and_indexing: All theorem sums run from j=0 through j=n, so they contain n+1 terms. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
The direct weight excludes k=j from its product over the interpolation nodes. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2)]
The exact linear coefficients are 3n+4 for the data-dependent term and 3n+2 for the denominator-cancellation term. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]

The offset difference arises because the numerator path includes multiplication by f_j and the final quotient contributes one additional rounding counter, whereas the denominator path does not include that multiplication. [PDF p. 4 (printed p. 550), proof of Theorem 3.2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), uncollected and collected counter expressions]
higher_order_terms: The result explicitly retains an additive O(u^2) term in every displayed form of the bound. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
The cited passage supplies no explicit coefficient, sign, or dependence on n, nodes, data, or condition numbers for the O(u^2) remainder. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
exceptional_values: The cited floating-point model does not explicitly discuss overflow, underflow, subnormal values, infinities, NaNs, or division by zero. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model through Lemma 3.1]

Formula (4.1) contains divisions by x-x_j and a final division by the computed denominator, but the cited passage gives no explicit x=x_j branch or zero-computed-denominator branch. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1) and computed-expression display]

The relative error and cond(x,n,f) are undefined when p_n(x)=0; Definition 2.1 explicitly restricts the condition number to p_n(x) nonzero, although Theorem 4.1 does not repeat the restriction in words. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]

undebatable_constraints: The selected algorithm is the second or proper barycentric formula (4.1), not the first-form modified Lagrange formula (3.1). [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1) and surrounding text]
There are n+1 data values and distinct nodes, indexed j=0,...,n. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph]
The analyzed weights are the direct weights w_j=1/product_{k!=j}(x_j-x_k), with computed relative-error counter angle(2n)_j. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2) and Lemma 3.1]
The forward bound must retain both terms: (3n+4)u cond(x,n,f) and (3n+2)u cond(x,n,1). [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eq. (4.3)]
The second term is equivalently the absolute-sum over absolute-sum denominator-cancellation ratio in equation (4.2). [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eq. (4.2)]
The remainder O(u^2) is part of the claimed result and cannot be silently dropped. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
The error notion is relative forward error normalized by |p_n(x)|, so the claim requires p_n(x) nonzero. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
The condition number uses componentwise relative perturbations of f. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1]
The constant-one argument in cond(x,n,1) denotes interpolation data identically equal to 1. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
The theorem includes an existential constant-factor sharpness assertion for rounding errors. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
The interval restriction x_j in [-1,1] is not a hypothesis of Theorem 4.1. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), paragraph introducing the later Lebesgue-constant analysis]

ambiguities.issue: The domain at interpolation nodes is not stated explicitly. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1)]
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (4.1) divides each term by x-x_j, but neither equation (4.1) nor Theorem 4.1 states x!=x_j or specifies the usual special return f_j when x=x_j. [PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1); PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
ambiguities.impact: A formal contract must either restrict x away from every node or separately specify node evaluation; silently treating the displayed quotient as defined at x=x_j would exceed the cited statement.

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point outcomes are omitted. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1)]
ambiguities.evidence: The model gives only relative-error equations for basic operations and does not mention overflow, underflow, subnormals, NaNs, infinities, division by zero, or a computed denominator that rounds to zero. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model through Lemma 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), computed quotient]
ambiguities.impact: Applicability to IEEE exceptional cases cannot be inferred; the relative model effectively covers only operations for which the stated finite relative-error representation is valid.

ambiguities.issue: The O(u^2) remainder is not quantitatively specified. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem writes only O(u^2), with no explicit bound, coefficient, sign, uniformity statement, or dependence on n, f, x, and the nodes. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)]
ambiguities.impact: The paper passage supports a first-order asymptotic contract, not an exact finite-u inequality obtained by deleting or assigning a coefficient to the remainder.

ambiguities.issue: The sharpness quantifiers and constant are not specified. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper states only that there exist rounding errors attaining the bound within a constant factor; it does not state the factor, its parameter dependence, or whether the assertion applies uniformly to every admissible problem instance. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
ambiguities.impact: The existential sharpness sentence must not be strengthened to a universal lower bound or to a claim with a particular numerical constant.

ambiguities.issue: The generic smallness assumption ku<1 is not instantiated in Theorem 4.1. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), definition of gamma_k; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
ambiguities.evidence: Page 549 assumes ku<1 for the generic gamma_k counter bound, while the theorem later uses counter lengths 3n+4 and 3n+2 without restating a corresponding explicit condition. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), gamma_k paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), collected counter expression; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization may need an explicit small-u hypothesis, but the source passage does not unambiguously choose its strongest required index.

ambiguities.issue: The theorem does not verbally restate p_n(x)!=0. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.1 defines cond(x,n,f) only for p_n(x)!=0, and Theorem 4.1 itself divides by |p_n(x)| while omitting a separate hypothesis line. [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Definition 2.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1]
ambiguities.impact: Nonvanishing is necessarily inherited for the displayed relative statement, but its status is contextual rather than an explicitly repeated theorem hypothesis.

contract_plain_english: For n+1 distinct floating-point nodes x_j, floating-point data f_j, and a floating-point evaluation point x, directly compute the barycentric weights and evaluate the second or proper barycentric quotient (4.1). [PDF p. 2 (printed p. 548), Section 2 opening paragraph; PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), eq. (3.2) and Lemma 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), eq. (4.1)] Under the stated standard relative floating-point model, and where the displayed divisions and relative error are defined, the computed value has numerator error counters of length 3n+4 and denominator counters of length 3n+2. [PDF p. 3 (printed p. 549), floating-point model; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 551), computed-expression display] Its relative forward error is at most (3n+4)u cond(x,n,f) plus (3n+2)u cond(x,n,1), plus O(u^2); the second condition number is the cancellation measure for the quotient denominator and uses constant-one data. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), Theorem 4.1 and eqs. (4.2)-(4.3)] The paper also claims constant-factor attainability for some rounding errors, without specifying the factor or full quantifiers. [PDF p. 6 (printed p. 552), sentence following eq. (4.3)]
